data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Suppression is not a property of the allocation policy but of the vocabulary inheritance mechanism. If a lineage can adopt a rival's primitive after encountering it (open inheritance), ownership is efficient. If it cannot (closed inheritance), ownership is suppressive. The evidence is the adoption rate.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If rival lineages are never tested on the same problems, A is trivially 0 and the test is inconclusive.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If adoption is delayed (the primitive is adopted in a successor artifact, not the current one), A may be undercounted in a single run.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the cost of adoption is higher than re-derivation, a low A may indicate efficiency, not suppression.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The allocation policy (ownership) only determines *who* sees the problem first. Whether this suppresses cross-cutting explanations depends on what happens *after* a rival solution is found. If the owning lineage can adopt the rival's primitive, the policy is efficient (it routes problems but does not block ideas). If it cannot, the policy is suppressive (it routes problems and blocks ideas). The observable evidence is the adoption rate. Count A = number of times an owning lineage adopts a rival primitive after a broadcast test. If A=0 (or A << S, where S is rival-success events), the inheritance mechanism is closed and suppression is systematic.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
